nameStory: The eerie name "Dead Man's Fingers" comes from this seaweed's appearance when washed up on shore - dark green, spongy branches that look disturbingly like decomposing fingers reaching up from the sand. The scientific name Codium fragile literally means "fragile fleece," referring to its soft, felt-like texture that breaks apart easily when handled.
description: Dead Man's Fingers is a distinctive green seaweed that looks like a dark green sponge with branching, finger-like projections. This marine algae forms clumps of thick, cylindrical branches that can grow up to a foot tall, though most specimens are smaller. Unlike typical flat seaweeds, it has a three-dimensional, almost coral-like structure with a soft, velvety surface that feels like wet felt when touched.

idTips.label: Spongy branching structure
idTips.description: Thick, cylindrical branches that fork repeatedly, creating a hand-like appearance with multiple "fingers" - soft and spongy to the touch, not flat like typical seaweeds

idTips.label: Felt-like texture
idTips.description: Surface feels like wet velvet or felt when touched - distinctly soft and fuzzy rather than smooth or slimy like other seaweeds

idTips.label: Dark green color
idTips.description: Deep forest green color that may appear almost black when wet, becoming lighter green when dried out on shore

idTips.label: Fragile consistency
idTips.description: Breaks apart easily when squeezed or pulled - pieces crumble off in your hands rather than tearing in sheets

idTips.label: No obvious holdfast
idTips.description: Often found loose on beaches without visible roots or attachment points, as it readily breaks free from its anchoring base

habitat: Found along rocky coastlines, tide pools, and sandy beaches throughout New England's Atlantic coast, particularly in Maine, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. Look for it attached to rocks and shells in shallow waters, or more commonly washed up on beaches after storms. It thrives in both protected coves and more exposed coastal areas.

seasonality.spring: Active growing season begins, with fresh specimens more likely to be found attached in tide pools and shallow waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season - look for the largest, most robust specimens both in water and freshly washed ashore.
seasonality.fall: Storm season brings many specimens onto beaches, though they may be more fragmented and weathered.
seasonality.winter: Still present but growth slows; beach specimens are often dark and deteriorated but still identifiable by texture and branching pattern.

funFact: This innocent-looking seaweed has earned the nickname "oyster thief" because it grows so densely on oyster shells that it acts like a sail, causing entire oyster beds to be ripped up and swept away by ocean currents - sometimes destroying entire commercial oyster farms overnight!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small pieces of sea sponge or coral, but Dead Man's Fingers is always green (sponges are usually tan, orange, or purple) and has that distinctive felt-like texture. Remember: if it's green, branchy, and feels like wet velvet, you've found Dead Man's Fingers.
contextualKnowledge: This seaweed is actually an invasive species that traveled from Japan to New England, likely hitchhiking on ship hulls or in ballast water. Despite its creepy name and invasive status, it's not harmful to touch and is even edible in some cultures, though it's quite tough and not particularly tasty.
compareHints: Dead Man's Fingers is the only Codium species commonly found in New England waters, making it relatively easy to identify within its genus. When comparing to other green seaweeds, it's unique in its three-dimensional, spongy structure - most other green marine algae are either flat sheets (like sea lettuce) or thin branching filaments, rather than these thick, finger-like projections.
